definition: Ordinary or lacking imagination and poetic beauty.
example: The trip ended for the prosaic reason that their car needed repairs.
nuance: Prosaic evaluates the character of something, not merely its literary format.
prompt: The mystery turns out to have a mundane explanation.
options: The missing lights had a prosaic explanation: someone had unplugged the cable.
The prosaic explanation involved a startling, imaginative vision of another world.
The explanation was prosaic simply because it appeared in prose rather than verse.
The prosaic detective solved dozens of strange mysteries every single year.
reasons: This sentence demonstrates the meaning: ordinary or lacking imagination and poetic beauty.
A startling imaginative vision is not mundane.
Writing in prose does not necessarily make its content dull or ordinary.
This confuses prosaic with prolific; producing a lot of work is not the same as being dull.

practice.prompt: A town council picks a name for its new neighborhood park.
options: The prosaic entrance was built from thousands of tiny colored tiles.
Most residents were prosaic about the park and voted eagerly to support it.
The council skipped the fanciful ideas and chose the prosaic name Third Street Park.
Children thought the name was prosaic because it sounded like a spell from a fairy tale.
reasons: This confuses prosaic with mosaic; a pattern of tiles has nothing to do with being dull.
Prosaic does not mean being in favor of something; eager support is not plainness.
A plain, practical name picked over imaginative ones shows the dull ordinariness the word conveys.
A name that sounds magical is whimsical and imaginative, the reverse of prosaic.
